claims.text: Elevated-temperature wear-corrosion causes degradation beyond the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only effects in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The accelerated degradation operates through a positive feedback between mechanical wear and corrosion.
Wear repeatedly disrupts a fragile, thermally formed oxide or passive film at heterogeneous phase boundaries.
Film disruption exposes fresh surfaces that are galvanically active.
The newly exposed surfaces are more susceptible to localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion subsequently accelerates mechanical wear.
The initial alloy has distinct interpenetrating phases.
A thermally formed but fragile oxide or passive film initially protects the alloy and covers its phase boundaries.
Heterogeneous interphase boundaries are the local sites where film disruption creates galvanic interactions.
At elevated temperature, a protective oxide film forms on each phase.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes the oxide film at phase boundaries.
Compositional differences between the phases create galvanic activity after fresh metal is exposed.
Galvanic activity accelerates localized corrosion at the interphase regions.
Localized corrosion embrittles the interphase regions.
Embrittlement of interphase regions increases their susceptibility to mechanical wear.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will cause greater overall material loss than either isolated exposure or exposure under conditions where the film remains stable.
Simultaneous exposure will increase corrosion pit formation at phase boundaries.
Simultaneous exposure will increase wear damage at phase boundaries.
The proposed mechanism requires mechanical loading sufficient to remove the protective film without completely disintegrating the material.
The proposed mechanism specifically depends on microstructural heterogeneity between the eutectic phases.
